definition: A system that records snapshots of a project over time, so you can see what changed, when and why, return to earlier versions, and combine work from several people.
A project's complete history and settings, stored in the hidden .git folder; it holds every commit, branch and tag, and is created with git init or git clone.
A recorded snapshot of every tracked file, with an author, date, message and a pointer to its parent commit. Its ID is a hash of all of that, so it never changes.
The project files on disk that you open and edit. Git compares them with the index and the last commit to report what has changed.
The next commit being assembled. git add copies a file's current content into it, git commit turns it into a commit, and git restore --staged takes content back out.
A file in the working tree that Git has never recorded and that isn't staged. It stays out of commits until you git add it, and .gitignore can hide it.
Git history as a directed acyclic graph: each commit points to its parent or parents, and following those links backwards from any commit gives its history.
A commit with two parents, created when Git combines two branches that have both moved on. Its snapshot contains the work from both lines of history.
A named, movable pointer to one commit. Committing while on a branch moves it forward to the new commit; creating one copies no files.
Git's pointer to where you are. It usually names the current branch, which names a commit; HEAD~1 means the commit before the one you're on.
The state where HEAD points straight at a commit instead of a branch. New commits made there belong to no branch until you create one with git switch -c.
A merge where the current branch hasn't moved since the other branch started, so Git simply slides the pointer forward and creates no merge commit.
The most recent commit two branches share. Git compares each branch tip with it during a three-way merge to decide which changes to take.
What happens when both branches changed the same lines since their merge base. Git writes both versions between markers and waits for you to edit, git add and continue.
Replaying a branch's commits on top of another commit, producing new commits with new IDs and a linear history. Safe only for commits nobody else has built on.
A force-push that only overwrites the remote branch if it still points where you last saw it, so you won't silently erase commits someone else pushed since your last fetch.
A named URL for another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub. origin is the conventional name for the one you cloned from or push to.
A local, read-only record such as origin/main of where a branch was on a remote at your last fetch, pull or push. It moves only when you talk to the remote.
The remote branch a local branch tracks, set with git push -u. It lets plain git push and git pull work and lets git status report ahead and behind counts.
Two linked keys used to prove who you are to GitHub: the private key stays on your machine, and the .pub public key is added to your GitHub account.
A GitHub proposal to merge one branch into another, where reviewers comment, automated checks run, and the change is finally merged. New pushes to the branch update it.
Your own copy of someone else's repository on GitHub. You push branches to it and open pull requests back to the original, conventionally called upstream.
A command that creates a new commit applying the exact opposite of an earlier commit. It undoes changes without rewriting history, so it's safe on shared branches.
A local log of every position HEAD has had, such as commits, resets, rebases and switches. It lets you find and restore commits that no branch points to any more.
A place to park uncommitted changes and get a clean working tree. git stash push saves them, git stash pop brings them back; add -u to include untracked files.
A file listing patterns of untracked files Git should never track, such as node_modules/, build output and .env. It doesn't affect files that are already tracked.
A commit message format, type(optional scope): description, using types like feat, fix and docs, so tools can generate changelogs and semantic version numbers.
A permanent, named marker on a commit that also stores the tagger, date and a message. Created with git tag -a, it's the usual way to mark a release.
A YAML file in .github/workflows/ that runs jobs on GitHub's machines when events like pull_request happen. Each job reports a status check on the pull request.
A named set of GitHub rules for branches or tags, such as requiring a pull request, requiring status checks to pass and blocking force pushes on main.
